messages.body_plain:
Pablo,

model.avg( ) is part of package MuMIn, you should ask the package maintainer for help on that function.

Otherwise, you might want to try modavg( ) in package AICcmodavg, for model averaging beta estimates, with something like this:

library(unmarked)
library(AICcmodavg)

data(linetran)

ltUMF <- with(linetran, {
  unmarkedFrameDS(y = cbind(dc1, dc2, dc3, dc4),
                  siteCovs = data.frame(Length, area, habitat),
                  dist.breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20),
                  tlength = linetran$Length * 1000, survey = "line", unitsIn = "m")
})

## Halfnormal. Covariates affecting both density and and detection.
fm2 <- distsamp(~area + habitat ~ habitat, ltUMF)
fm3 <- distsamp(~area + habitat ~ habitat, ltUMF, keyfun="hazard")

Cands <- list(fm1, fm2, fm3)
Modnames <- paste("mod", 1:length(Cands), sep = "")

modavg(Cands, Modnames, parm = "habitatB", parm.type = "lambda")

Best,

Marc

I think this might just be a case of putting the right object into the mod.avg()function.

You have:

model.avg(fms2,subset=delta < 2)

Where fms2 is a fitList and not a modSel object so there is no delta to be used for the subsetting <- source of error. So try this out:

ms1 <- modSel(fms2)

model.avg(ms1,subset=delta < 2)

Sorry for delay in my response having asked to see a bit more. I hope that helps…?

Chris

Hi Matt,

unmarked returns AIC rather than AICc because it is not clear, to me
at least, what the effective sample size is for these models. I think
this issue was discussed in a previous thread and in the MacKenzie et
al 2005 book.

As for model averaging, see help(fitList). Basically, you put your
models in a fitList object, and then you use predict:

fmList <- fitList(m1, m2, m3, etc...)  # put models in a fitList object
predict(fmList, type="state")            # expected values for
original data. or,
predict(fmList, type="state", newdata = somenewdata)

This will give you model-averaged predictions and SEs. We have
intentionally not provided capabilities for model-averaging beta
coefficients or variance-covariance matrices.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

I've been running a couple N-mixture models for some Swiss songbird data using pcount and assessed goodness of fit using a parametric bootstrap. For the Poisson mixture, I usually find that the model does not fit. Now I am interested in quantifying the degree of lack of fit, similar as the capture-recapture folks do when they compute their c-hat.

Under the hypothesis that all lack of fit is some unstructured kind of "overdispersion", c-hat is the factor by which the variance needs to be inflated (therefore, the SEs need to be made larger by a factor of sqrt(c-hat)). Regardless of whether one thinks that this procedure is valid/useful or not, I find it useful to quantify the degree to which the data depart from the assumed model.

So I was wondering how a c-hat could be computed for Nmix models ? I assume I can take the observed value of a chisquare test statistic and divide that by the mean of the bootstrap distribution of that statistic. ---  Any comments are welcome.

Kind regards  --  Marc

Hi All,

I'm hoping to get some feedback on whether or not an open abundance model is appropriate for my data. We're trying to estimate density, and we have repeated counts from visual surveys of small mammals (ground squirrels and prairie dogs) along 1-km transects for three summers. In the first summer, we performed one survey, and in summers two and three we did two surveys per transect, each about a month apart. Does the population need to be closed within summers?  I think mortality is fairly high, and I can imagine that some of our sample has been eaten by the time we return for the second survey in a summer.   We also recorded the distance to each detection, so maybe distance sampling would be better? I think that the Chandler et al (2011) model accounts for temporary emigration, but not demographic factors, so I'm not sure it's appropriate here.

Any input would be appreciated!

Lucretia

Dear all,

I've been running N-mix model analyses for some Swiss songbirds and compared all three mixture distributions available in pcount() in terms of AIC and GOF (the latter by parametric bootstrap). The ZIP mixture models fit best overall and so I want to use them to predict expected abundance in relation to the modelled environmental covariates and also map those predictions for all of Switzerland (i.e., produce a species distribution map).

hi Pablo,

I find that this is an interesting application for occupancy modeling and, btw, it is the „opposite“ of what people have done for estimating the proportion of sites where some species is still extant among a list of sites that were known to be occupied at some earlier time („revisitation studies“, mostly for plants). There is an alternative framework for occupancy estimation with single reps and strong covariate information which you may want to look into; see a series of papers by Lele, Moreno, Solymos.

Hi unmarked users--

I'm having trouble running some temporary emigration models using gpcount. To test it out, I'm starting by analyzing 2 seasons of data. Each season consists of 5 sampling periods, and I'm assuming the time frame is short enough to have demographic closure. I'm working with terrestrial salamanders, which move back-and-forth vertically from the ground surface to underground retreats, and we know this movement is related to weather variables, such as recent rainfall. In the help for gpcount, it says "This model is also applicable to sampling designs in which the local population size is closed during the J repeated counts, and availability is related to factors such as the probability of vocalizing. In this case, density can be estimated by M(i)/plotArea." My interpretation is that instead of "probability of vocalizing," I have "probability of being on the surface."

Here is my code for creating the frame...

y.2011.umf <- unmarkedFrameGPC(y=counts,
                               siteCovs=data.frame(lfi=lfi.z, tsi=tsi.z, slope=slope.z,
